Indian Standard
GUIDELINES FOR PLANNING, LAYOUT AND DESIGN OF CAVITIES UNDERGROUND HYDROELECTRTC POWER STATIONS 0. FOREWORD IN

0.1 This Indian Standard was adopted by the Indian Standards Institution on 29 March 1979, after the draft finalized by the Hydro-Electric Power House Structures Sectional Committee had been approved by the Civil Engineering Division Council.
0.2 With the progressive harnessing of the hydroelectric potential in the country an increasingly large number of underground hydroelectric power stations are being built. These stations are housed in underground cavities in order to utilize the available head :Lt places where surface hydroclcctric power station construction is not possible. The importance of laying down guidelines for planning and layout of these cavities is evident considering the huge investment being made in coustructing underground hydroelectric power stations and the economy that can be effected by following these guidelines.

Service bay and control room may bc Iocated in lirle with the machine hall. While this arrangement limits the size of individual cavities and leads to a greater safety in the case of fire hazards or pipe burst, the volume of excavation increases and separate erection cranes are required in the parallel cavities. 4

3.1.6 With a view to limiting the size of the cavity and to meet with the specific geological conditions, the relative layout of the control valves, machine hall, transformer hall, service bay and control room may find great variations. As such each underground power station tends to be individualistic in its layout, Further changes from the originally planned layout may be necessary to cope with the adverse geological features met with as the excavation progresses. 3.2 The location of the transformers in the underground cavity is a matter of pure economics, as insulation of high tension cables does not pose a problem. 3.3 The machine hall cavity housing the generating units is the single largest cavity in an underground power station and utmost care and Some of the possible ways in planning shall be exercised to limit its size. which this may be done are as follows, depending upon the rock condition: a) Adoption b) Recessing c) Lifting of larger units. columns partly into the side walls. beam permitting the than by shaft. the power station

3.4 Access to power station may be provided through vertical shafts and inclined galleries. For use in emergency, provision of alternative route through tunnels,/shafts provided for cables, ventilation, etc, should also be considered. 3.5 Cables ( high tension or low tension ) from the transformer/generating unit to surface switchyard may be carried in cable tunnels or vertical shaft. 3.6 Air for ventilation cable-cum-ventilation may be drawn through separate ventilation tunnel or access-cum-ventilation shaft. tunnels,

3.7 A collection gallery or a downstream surge tank may be required for meeting fluctuation in discharge as a result of load variation, specially if there is a long tail race tunnel. 11

IS z 9120 - 1979 4. DATA REQUIRED plan of the area;

4.1 The following data shall be collected: a) Topographic b) Surface and subsurface geological plan of the area; c) Log charts of drifts, boreholes and open excavation; d) Evaluation of mechanical defects in the geological structure of rock, such as folds and associated fractures, faults and related crushing and fracturing; joints, their spacing and pattern; other weakness such as cleavage, bedding plane schistosity, slip plane shear plane, etc; e) Inferred geology along the proposed cavities; f) Depth of unconsolidated material or solid rock; g) Topography and its relation to attaining desired depth of cover; and h) Ground water assessment, such as presence of aquifers aqaifuges, chemical properties of water; j) Water pressure tests on representative rock of cavity;

k) Grout pressure versus grout mix curve; m) Physical properties of rock and ofmaterial filling rock joints; n) In-situ Young's Modulus of rock, its shear strength and coefficient of sliding friction; p) In-situ internal rock stresses; q) Pull out tests on rock bolts and test on installation of grouted anchors; r) Size and dimension of construction equipment, such as pulling unit with the trailer and its turning radius, size ofjumbos, size of the largest piece of equipment required to be carried into the cavity; maximum gradient on which the equipment can move, etc; such as dimensions of unit bays, s) Hydroelectric requirements, service bay, control room, transformer hall, if underground, mode of carrying generator terminal connection and high tension or low tension cables, detailed layout of equipment in the power station alongwith their loads and point of application, air conditioning and ventilation arrangement, lighting arrangement; and t) Photoelastic model tests for determining cavity for various stages of excavation. 5. ROCK COVER stress field around the

5.1 Effective rock cover below the line of slumping should be provided depending upon the condition of rock. 12

IS : 9120 .I979

6. ALfGNMENT 6.1 An underground

OF CAVITIES

power station involves excavation of large number of cavities within the rockmass. The rock in which the cavities may be located should be massive and least jointed, hard and of a quality competent to sustain a large opening.

6.2 The largest rock span and mcst difficult part of the excavation within The machine hall may be oriented in the power station is the machine hall. that direction which utilizes to the greatest extent the rock arching action. This is normally achieved by aligning the cavity in a direction normal to the rock strike. However, where tile joints, slip planes and seams are numerous, a detailed statistical survey of the ruling joint pattern and orientation of the seams may be carried out and as much regard should be given to these significant discontinues in the rock mass as to the strike of the rock itself. The machine hall cavity may be aligned on the basis of an optimum compromise between the direction of the ruling strike and the direction of such features so as to ensure that inferior rock formation is confined to the shortest dimension of the cavity. 6.3 Changes in originally planned Lyout may become obligatory arising from knowledge of rock condition encountered during actual excavation of the cavity. 7. SHAPE OF

CAVITY

7.1 The underground rock is under stress mainly due to the weight of the An underground opening due overlying rock and due to tectonic stresses. to redistribution of the existing rock stresses causes stress concentration in Analysis of stresses around the opening the rock surrounding the opening. is greatly handicapped due to heterogeneous character of rock mass, irregularities in the boundaries, presence of numerous fissures and slide plane;, lack of knowledge of initial state of stress in the rock mass and the rock bchaviour under elastic and plastic conditions. The initial state of stresses within the rock mass is best determined from in-situ tests. The best shape of cavity for the power station is one which gives the least stress concentration and does not lead to development of tension around the opening. 8. ROCK COVER BETWEEN CAVITIES

8.1 Adequate rock cover between two cavities shall be provided depending upon the quality and the strength of the rock in which the cavities are located. 13

9.3 The structural behaviour of roof arch depends upon the extent to which Should the arch become tile arch has become an integral part of the rock. au integral part of the rock, the superimposed loads will be mostly radial In practice, resulting in only compressive stresses in the arch section. however, the behaviour of the roof arch will be in between the following two limiting conditions: a) Integral part of the rock, and free from rock except at the abutments. fixed and of the arch may be taken as between b) Completely hinged.

9.3.1 The end conditions

9.4 Rock bolting has been extensively employed as means of providing temporary and permanent support to the roof of the power station cavity. Rock bolt spacing shall be close and their length may be kept at least equal to the radius of the opening or double the depth of the fractured zone.

SUPPORTS

OF CAVITY

10.1 Wide range of treatment to the walls have to be carried out in the underground power station dependin g mainly on the quality of the rock. The design of wall shall depend on such troatment.

GROUTING

11.1 The

purpose of grouting is to improve upon rock deformabiiity and strength, close up seams, joints, cracks, etc, so as to develop, as far as possiblc, a strong homogeneous impermeable shell of rock mass around the cavity. The factors which merit attention are the following dcpendiug upon site condition for the type of rock on the basis of in-situ test: a) Grout b) Grout c) Depth, mix, pressure, spacing and and size of grout holes.

12. DRAINAGE 12.1 The purpose of drainage is to decrease the uplift and seepage pressures and increase the stability of the rock mass around the cavity correspondingly. Draingc is affected through holes in the roof andwalls of the cavity. 13. STRESS RELIEVING

of high stresses occurring at sharp boundary corners, it may become necessary to adopt stress relieving measures at these points. The stress relieving may be effected by drilling stress relieving slots.

APPENDIX ( Chuse 9.2.1 )
ROCK A-l. A-l.1 GENERAL LOADS

A

ON POWER HOUSE

ROOF

No method is yet available for correct assessment of rock loads likely to be imposed on roof element. Varying and complex nature of rock reduces the usefulness of the otherwise simple method of cvalllating rock loads, based mainly on the natural arch theory and Fenner's profile of no tension ellipse. Accordingly, it becomes necessary to evaluate rock loads by all possible methods, and to adopt design loads after their due considerations and the nature of the rock.
16

IS I9120
A-2. TRIANGULAR LOADING METHOD

- 1979

A-2.1 In the triangular loading method, it is assumed that the rock loads would correspond to the weight of the rock confined within a triangle with side sloping at ( 45-$/2 ) with the vertical, where + is angle of internal friction and may be taken at 40" for crushed rock mass in absence of relevant data. This method is analogous with lintal design. A-3. FENNER'S ELLIPSE METHOD

A-3.1 Fcnner's ellipse method assumes that failure occurs along an elliptical surface enveloping the opening and passing through springing of The rock loads on the roof are due to the weight of the rock the arch. between the ellipse and the roof intrados, For massive moderately jointed rock, the ellipse may be drawn for no tension condition. For blocky and seamy rock, the ellipse may be drawn for the boundary tangential stress equal to that existing prior to excavation of the cavity. A-4.

NORWEGIAN

METHOD

A-4.1 `The Norwegian method consists of drawing a parabola from the springing of the roof and considering the rock load as due to the weight of the rock between the parabola and the roof intrados. In most of the cases, angle of the tangent at the abutment is about 40". 17
